title: Flexibility
subtitle: Stretch with a purpose, a suitable dose, and fewer dramatic negotiations

blocks.text: This lesson is general education, not diagnosis, treatment or rehab. Get qualified advice before stretching a fresh injury, a joint that was recently operated on, a joint that gives way, or an area with pain, numbness, weakness or swelling you can’t explain. Follow advice for your condition if you have osteoporosis, a joint replacement, loose joints, a nerve condition, a pregnancy or a disability. Stop and get urgent medical help for sudden nerve symptoms, a serious fall, a joint that looks out of shape, or suddenly being unable to put weight on a leg.

Before stretching, you’ll answer four questions. What’s the goal? Which area is limiting it? What type of stretch fits? How did your body respond? This keeps you from collecting stretches as if the body gave out loyalty points.
Spend less time stretching and get more out of every minute.
blocks.detail: Picking the right stretch for a real goal, at the right dose and time, gives you comfort and range you can use.
blocks.extra: Section 04 shows how long and how hard to stretch.

blocks.text: Flexibility is the range a joint can move through, or how well muscles and other tissues handle being lengthened. It can make a task more comfortable when that task needs more range than you have right now.

Choose a specific reason: reaching overhead, taking a longer stride when you walk, holding a work position, a sports skill, or easing the stiff feeling after sitting for a long time. The range you aim for should match the activity.

Flexibility isn’t a complete fitness program. Strength, balance, stamina, coordination, sleep and daily movement still matter. You can touch your toes and still be unprepared to carry the recycling downstairs.
Record the movement you want to make more comfortable. A stretch without a purpose is difficult to evaluate.

items.title: “Everyone should be able to touch their toes.”
items.text: Body proportions, joint shape, nerve sensitivity, skill and training history all differ. Touching your toes is one movement, not a health certificate.

blocks.text: Name your flexibility goal
Finish this sentence: “I want more comfortable range for ___.”

Dynamic flexibility uses controlled movement through a comfortable range. Examples are controlled leg swings, arm circles, walking lunges and gentle trunk turns. Dynamic work warms you up and rehearses the moves you’re about to use.

Static stretching holds a position for a while. Use it in a separate flexibility session or after activity, when the goal is to practise relaxed range. You should be able to breathe normally, with no sharp pain or nerve symptoms.

Before strength work, sprinting or sport, start with easy whole-body movement and dynamic moves that match the task. Long, intense static stretches right before an all-out effort may briefly reduce force or power for some activities. Short holds of under a minute have little effect. Time your stretching to suit what comes next.
Use movement to prepare for movement. Use longer holds when gaining or keeping range is the main job.
Move slowly into a mild-to-moderate stretch feeling. Stop before sharp pain, pinching, burning, numbness, tingling or a joint feeling unstable. Breathe normally and don’t bounce.

A short hold repeated a few times can help. The best length and frequency depend on you, the tissue, your goal and any advice you’ve had. The stretch should be repeatable and shouldn’t get in the way of whatever you do next.
A common starting dose

items.title: Hold
items.text: 10 to 30 seconds — at a mild-to-moderate stretch feeling.

items.title: Repeat
items.text: 2 to 4 times — for about 60 seconds in total per stretch.

items.title: How often
items.text: At least 2 or 3 days a week — daily practice works best for gaining range.

blocks.text: Progress with a slightly longer comfortable hold, another repeat, a better position or stretching more often. Change one thing at a time. The muscle doesn’t need a surprise party.

items.title: “A stretch only works if it hurts.”
items.text: Pain can make muscles tense up to protect you, and it may signal irritation or injury. A tolerable stretch feeling is enough.

sections.title: Use Position to Target the Right Area

blocks.text: Small setup changes can shift a stretch away from the muscle you want and into a joint or another area. Use support and steady alignment. Keep the movement in the joint’s comfortable path.

For a calf stretch, the direction of your foot and keeping your heel down matter. For the hip, your pelvis and trunk position matter. For the chest, your shoulder position matters. For the back of the thigh, bending from the hip is different from rounding your whole spine.

Don’t copy the deepest-looking version. Choose the one that gives the feeling you want without joint pressure or losing control. The internet’s most flexible person isn’t there to sign your consent form.
Adjust your stance, support or angle. A better position often gives a clearer stretch with less effort.

sections.title: Know When Stretching Is the Wrong Tool

blocks.text: A tight feeling isn’t always a flexibility problem. Tired or weak muscles, an irritated joint, a sensitive nerve, swelling, stress, poor sleep, holding one position for a long time or new activity can all feel like tightness.

If a few gentle moves ease the feeling, more variety in your movement may be enough. If the same spot keeps feeling tight during a task, check your technique, workload, strength and setup. If you have tingling, numbness, weakness, a lot of swelling, a joint giving way or pain that’s getting worse, get it checked.
Hypermobility means some joints move further than usual. People with hypermobility who have symptoms may need control, strength, pacing and personal care, rather than more stretching.

items.title: “Every tight feeling should be stretched.”
items.text: The feeling can have several causes. Stretching only helps when limited range or tissue tolerance is part of the real problem.

blocks.text: Sophie stops stretching everything
paragraphs: Sophie, 44, worked at a computer in Montreal. By late afternoon her neck and shoulders felt tight, so every evening she followed a fifteen-minute full-body stretching video. Some stretches felt nice, but the same discomfort was back before dinner the next day.

One Friday, her physiotherapist friend asked a simple question: when does it start? Sophie realized she had never checked. She could keep stretching harder, or she could spend one week watching for the pattern. She chose to watch.

The pattern was clear. The discomfort grew after long, unbroken stretches at the screen. Her monitor sat off to one side, so she turned her head all day, and her upper back tired out as the hours went by.

Sophie moved the monitor straight in front of her and set a reminder for short movement breaks. She practised gentle upper-back turns and shoulder moves, and added a light band row twice a week. She kept one chest stretch that helped and dropped the rest.

In week three, a deadline glued her to the desk for two days and the tightness came roaring back. It was tempting to restart the long video. Instead, she went back to the breaks, and within a few days the afternoons settled again.

After six weeks, she had fewer uncomfortable afternoons and could work longer before needing a break. Her routine shrank from fifteen minutes to four. The other eleven minutes went back to civilian life.

blocks.text: If a stretch has no clear target, no useful effect and doesn’t help your chosen task, it may not belong in your routine.
Find the real cause of the tightness, and you can fix it in minutes a day.
blocks.detail: Matching the tool to the problem, whether that’s a stretch, a strength move or a better setup, saves time and works better.
blocks.extra: Section 08 explains when to protect an area instead of stretching it.

sections.title: Protect Joints, Nerves, and Healing Tissue

blocks.text: Stretching should never force a healing injury, a joint that gives way or a sore surgical area. Follow the limits and plan from your treating professional. Scars, tendons, joints, muscles and nerves can each need a different approach.
Numbness, tingling, electric feelings, spreading pain or weakness may mean an irritated nerve. Don’t use a strong stretch to chase these symptoms. Stop and get a qualified assessment.
This section has no humour, because fresh injuries, unstable joints and nerve symptoms need clear care decisions.
Test your chosen task again under the same conditions. Can you reach, turn, step or hold the position more comfortably? Is the range easier to control? Did the change last after the stretch?
A quick gain right after stretching may just mean less tension or more tolerance. Lasting change takes repeated practice and using the new range. Strengthening that range helps make it useful.

Review every two to four weeks. Keep the stretch that helps, adjust one part of the dose, or swap the exercise if the task doesn’t improve. After illness, injury or a flare-up, go back to an easier version.

items.title: “A flexibility routine must keep getting deeper.”
items.text: Keeping your range may be the right goal. Useful range that supports your activities is worth more than more range for its own sake.

blocks.text: A good session should leave the area comfortable and usable. More range with irritation is not a winning trade.

Qualified help may be available through physiotherapy, occupational therapy, community health centres, rec programs, Indigenous health organizations, campuses and adapted exercise services. Public coverage, work benefits, referrals, regulation and wait times vary by province and territory.

CSEP professionals can guide your exercise within their training. Physiotherapists assess and treat movement and injury problems. Get qualified care when symptoms, surgery, unstable joints or a health condition affect your stretching choices.
Key takeaway
Flexibility work helps most when it serves a specific task, uses a tolerable dose and fits the timing and state of your body. Stretch for useful range, then practise control and strength there.
Save one photo or written setup cue for each stretch. “Left foot forward, heel down” beats rebuilding the pose from memory while leaning against a laundry basket.

items.title: What does flexibility describe?
items.detail: Available joint range or the tolerance of muscles and other tissues to lengthening.

items.title: How does flexibility differ from mobility?
items.detail: Mobility adds active control and the ability to use the range in a task.

items.title: When may dynamic movement fit better than a long static hold?
items.detail: Before exercise, sport, strength, or another activity requiring movement and force.

items.title: What sensations mean a stretch should stop?
items.detail: Sharp pain, pinching, burning, numbness, tingling, instability, or worsening symptoms.

items.title: Why should setup change before force increases?
items.detail: A better stance, support, or angle can target the intended area with less joint stress.

items.title: What helped Sophie's discomfort?
items.detail: Improved desk setup, movement breaks, upper-back and shoulder movement, rowing, and one focused stretch.

items.title: Why can hypermobility change the plan?
items.detail: More range may worsen instability; control, strength, pacing, and individual guidance may be needed.

items.title: What makes flexibility progress useful?
items.detail: It improves the named task or comfort and remains controllable without irritation.

blocks.text: Choose one flexibility goal. Try one suitable dynamic movement or static stretch, then retest the named task. Record the sensation during the exercise and the response later that day.
Skip any medical details or symptoms in this form. Just the plan.

items.title: Dynamic flexibility
items.text: Controlled movement through a range without a prolonged hold.

items.title: Flexibility
items.text: Available range or the ability of tissues to tolerate lengthening.

items.title: Hypermobility
items.text: Joint movement beyond a typical range, which may or may not cause symptoms.

items.title: Static stretch
items.text: A position held for a period of time to practise tissue tolerance or range.

items.title: Stretch tolerance
items.text: The level of lengthening sensation a person can comfortably accept.
